cards.title: Bill of Materials as the Foundation of Supply Chain Profit
cards.summary: A bill of material (BOM) is the foundational layer for any physical-goods business and the starting point for supply chain optimization and cash extraction.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing sourcing and COGS for a physical product store, or planning a cost-reduction or margin-improvement initiative across SKUs.
steps: Build a complete bill of materials for every sellable SKU: all components, packaging, inserts, and variable costs (shipping, duties, fees) that make up true landed cost.
Treat the BOM as the base of the profit pyramid — everything downstream (management accounts, free cash flow, distributions) depends on it being accurate.
For stores already doing millions in revenue, reconcile the BOM against actual supplier invoices and freight costs to find gaps and margin leaks.
Use the BOM to standardize margin accounting across all SKUs, and revisit it whenever a cost input (freight, packaging, supplier pricing) moves.
caveats: Speech-to-text garbled 'BOM' as 'bum' — the actual concept is bill of material.
The claim that BOM is 'by far' the most foundational input is the source's opinion, framed as advice to operators of physical goods.

cards.title: Free Cash Flow vs. Enterprise Value: Which Game Is Your Store Playing
cards.summary: Businesses should be mapped on a quadrant of free cash flow versus enterprise value, because cash extraction tactics and exit options differ entirely between the two.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to optimize a store for ongoing cash distributions versus building a sellable, valued enterprise.
steps: Map your business on two axes: free cash flow (money taken out monthly) and enterprise value (multiple a buyer would pay).
Recognize the classic dropship pattern — high free cash flow, near-zero enterprise value — and decide whether that is intentional or a trap.
If you want enterprise value, invest in brand, durable systems, management accounts, and audited financials rather than just ad arbitrage.
Note that with strong enterprise value you gain access to additional levers (like dividend recaps) that pure cash-flow businesses cannot pull.
caveats: The source asserts most online sellers 'are probably not a brand' — a strong opinion, not a measured fact.
No numeric thresholds define each quadrant; the framework is qualitative.

cards.title: Dividend Recap: Extracting Cash Without a Personal Guarantee (When Eligible)
cards.summary: A dividend recap lets a business borrow against itself and distribute proceeds to the owner, but requires substantial EBITDA history and carries covenants.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether your store can extract liquidity for owners without selling equity, typically after several years of consistent profit.
steps: Confirm eligibility: the source frames a realistic minimum as around $2M of EBITDA with 3 years of consistent history and the most recent year audited.
Approach a bank or lender and request a loan priced off EBITDA (source cites roughly 3x), with the proceeds distributed to owners rather than used for operations.

Factor in all-in effective cost — the source says a 10% headline rate can translate to 12–14% after fees, admin costs, breakage fees, and quality-of-earnings work; larger EBITDA (e.g., ~$10M) may get effective rates around 9–11%.
Account for tax treatment: interest is pre-tax, so a 10% rate may effectively be closer to 6–8% after evaluating the tax shield.
Expect lenders to prefer a new equity partner in some cases, and possibly partial recourse or personal guarantees.
caveats: Source notes this is best-case framing; many deals include recourse or personal guarantee on part of the money.
Covenants (e.g., interest coverage around 2x, sometimes as low as 1.5x for huge firms) can trigger breach and claw-back — do not use giant-firm benchmarks.
The source explicitly states this is not financial advice.

cards.title: How a Dividend Recap Blows Up: Interest Coverage Covenants
cards.summary: A recap fails when a covenant like interest coverage is breached, so operators must model the profit floor implied by their loan terms before borrowing.
cards.use_when: Stress-testing whether to take on debt against your store's profits, or modeling downside scenarios before signing a loan.
steps: Calculate your interest coverage ratio: EBITDA or profits divided by annual interest expense.
Identify the covenant threshold in the term sheet — the source describes a common ballpark of 2x coverage, sometimes negotiated lower.
Translate the covenant into an absolute profit floor: e.g., a $10M loan at 10% = $1M/year interest, requiring at least ~$2M in profits under a 2x covenant.
Model seasonal or category downturns and confirm you stay above the floor; if not, renegotiate the multiple or reduce leverage.
Remember breach can give the lender claw-back rights.
caveats: The 2x figure is described as a simplification and negotiable; do not treat it as a universal standard.

cards.title: Offer Optimization as the #1 Meta Scaling Lever
cards.summary: For most stuck Meta accounts, the biggest lever is a stale or weak offer rather than new creatives or bidding changes.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a paid-social account that has plateaued despite healthy spend, or planning a growth push on a store in the $5–50M range.
steps: Audit your current offers and ask whether they are aggressive and compelling enough for the category — the source says 90% of stuck accounts fail here.
Test offer constructs like buy-two-get-three, BOGO, free gifts at cart or checkout, and email-capture discounts.
Change offers before changing everything else — the source reports >50% lifts from offer changes alone with the same creatives.
Model the variable cost of each offer (extra units, packaging, dimensional weight shipping) and compute profit per visitor, not just revenue per visitor.
Test small discount deltas: the source says 10% vs 15% had zero impact, but 10% vs 20% showed a real delta.
caveats: The source's specific lift numbers come from their portfolio and are examples, not benchmarks.
Do not blankly increase offer aggressiveness — extra units can inflate shipping and fulfillment costs and shrink profit.

cards.title: Rotating Hooks and Angles Before Adding Media Budget
cards.summary: When the offer is solid but the account is stuck, the bottleneck is breadth of hooks and angles for the product.
cards.use_when: Scaling creative testing on Meta or planning a new creative sprint for a single hero SKU.
steps: Count how many distinct hooks and angles you currently run — the source says founders often stall at 3–4.
Recruit new angles from categories the product touches: use-case, occupation, gifting occasion, social proof, and objection handling.
Study outlier ads from adjacent categories for the opening frame, not just the product story (the source cites a personal-assistant gifting angle for jewelry).
Volume-test angles with consistent production sprints and kill losers quickly; expect only a fraction to print.
Feed the winning frameworks back into your production brief so new variants stay aligned with the proven promise.
caveats: Creative testing is not a substitute for a weak offer — the source treats offer as lever #1 and hooks as lever #2.
No fixed 'correct' hook count is given; the direction is 'more than 3–4.'

cards.title: Influencer-Specific Landing Pages That Mirror the Ad
cards.summary: Matching the ad to a personalized collection page in the same order the products appeared produced a large conversion lift.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding landing pages for influencer or whitelisted ads, or diagnosing a creative-to-page mismatch killing conversion.
steps: When an influencer ad promotes multiple products, build a dedicated collection page featuring their name, face, and code.
Order products on the landing page to match the chronological order they appeared in the ad.
Ensure the lead product or first-shown product sits above the fold on the collection page.
Add creator quote and lifestyle imagery where the page permits (e.g., supplements, single-product pages).
Test against your current generic collection pages and measure conversion rate.
caveats: The 30% conversion lift is a source-reported number from their own portfolio, not a universal benchmark.
The technique works best when the ad shows a finite product set; catalog mashup b-roll was said to underperform single- or aligned-product ads.

cards.title: Using Partnership Ads to Bridge the Trust Gap
cards.summary: Whitelisting creator content as partnership ads adds trust signals and diversity to a Meta account that standard brand ads cannot.
cards.use_when: Scaling paid social for high-AOV or considered-purchase products, or diversifying a Meta ad account dominated by brand-owned creatives.
steps: Give creators the ability to hand over ad code and page rights for their content (Meta's partnership ads, modeled on TikTok Spark ads).
Aim for a meaningful whitelisted share of your ad library — the source runs roughly 40–50% partnership content.
Lean on real, aged creator profiles so the ad reads as a person rather than a brand, which the source says matters especially for high-AOV products.
Compensate creators in ways that match your cash-flow discipline; the source uses fixed fees, often broken into a daily rate with a short cancellation or trial window (they cite ~10–14 days).
Alternatively test variable or percentage-of-spend compensation for select creators, recognizing it can create operational mess if terms are inconsistent.
caveats: The source says most operators were not running partnership ads at the time of recording — early-adopter framing, not proven universal performance.
Comparing fixed-fee vs. variable-fee compensation is unresolved in the source; each is presented as a situational alternative.

cards.title: Paying Creators a Trial Daily Rate Before Committing
cards.summary: Compensate whitelisted creators with a fixed daily rate and a short trial window so media spend is predictable and risk is bounded.
cards.use_when: Negotiating influencer or partnership-ad deals when you cannot forecast whether the asset will convert.
steps: Convert a monthly creator fee into a daily rate (e.g., source cites ~$10k/month broken into a daily figure).
Set a trial period (source references ~10–14 days) with a breakout or cancellation clause so you can stop paying if the creative does not perform.
Frame the deal transparently: you will pay the day rate, you want to see performance, and you want to manage risk.
Consider paying a modest kicker or higher rate during the trial period to reflect the creator's upfront production work.
Keep deal terms across creators consistent — the source says spread of terms across too many creators creates operational chaos.
caveats: The source notes they are still second-guessing this model versus variable compensation after seeing other operators pay much larger variable fees.
Daily rate, trial length, and kicker are source-specific to the source's portfolio; not universally applicable benchmarks.

cards.title: One-Day-Click ROAS with Post-Purchase Survey Multiplier
cards.summary: Use platform-independent 1-day click ROAS tempered by post-purchase survey data to extrapolate lifetime performance and judge whether an ad account can be scaled profitably.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale spend on Meta and other channels when multi-touch attribution is judged unreliable, especially for considered-purchase products.
steps: Track 1-day click ROAS in a cross-channel tool like Northbeam as your source of truth, since the platform-agnostic number is comparable across time.
Run a post-purchase survey asking 'when did you first hear of us' with bins like today, past week, past two weeks, month, six months, a year.
Assume the pessimistic case that only 1-day click conversions drove revenue — zero credit to view-through.
Multiply the immediate share (e.g., 20–25% for a jewelry brand) into 1-day click ROAS to estimate lifetime ROAS: a 0.5 one-day click implies roughly 2.0 lifetime under that assumption.
Compare the extrapolated lifetime ROAS against your breakeven ROAS to decide whether to keep scaling.
caveats: The percentages cited are sourced from their portfolio and seasons and are not benchmarks.
Northbeam's internal LTV calculations were not trusted by the source — they run the math themselves on top of the 1-day-click number.
The extrapolation is deliberately conservative (no view-through credit), which can understate performance in some windows.

cards.title: Post-Purchase Survey Questions Worth Copying
cards.summary: Post-purchase surveys can reveal acquisition source, timing, competitive set, and even who to book next as an influencer.
cards.use_when: Building or refreshing a post-purchase survey on Shopify to inform creative, media mix, and influencer booking decisions.
steps: Ask where the customer heard of you (channel, platform) and when (today, week, month, six months, year) to feed the 1-day-click multiplier.
Ask basic demographics relevant to your category (age, gender) for targeting and persona scoring.
Ask which other brands they considered before buying — useful for competitive creative and positioning work.
Ask which influencer should represent the brand — the source uses this field to find and book influencers.
Deploy via a lightweight Shopify survey app, run it continuously, and refresh the question set when new hypotheses emerge.
caveats: Customers do not always remember accurately — treat responses as directional evidence, not instrumentation.
The exact survey wording and app were referenced but not fully specified in the source; pick a compatible Shopify tool and verify current options.

cards.title: YouTube Influencer Strategy: Patience and Portfolio Math
cards.summary: YouTube influencer ad reads are a venture-style portfolio play that requires deep payback tolerance and CPM-by-cohort pricing across personas.
cards.use_when: Planning or scaling a YouTube influencer program for a physical product brand, especially ones with broad audiences.
steps: Accept long payback windows — the source notes YouTube payback can exceed 30 days, so the account must stomach slow returns.
Budget for portfolio outcomes: the source describes ~100 booked influencers where ~20 print and pay for the 80 that do not.
Build a CPM scorecard by persona (gamer, hobbyist, mom, etc.) so each creator is priced to expected value, not gut feel.
Back into profit: the source's true north star is whether a $10k placement can generate a defined dividend amount after all costs, not just ROAS.
Focus on persona-fit and production quality of the read — a great ad read on a compatible audience is what unlocks outlier CPM efficiency.
caveats: The source's own spend dropped from early years (~$20M) to steady-state (~$4–7M/year), so this is not a 'spend more' recommendation.
YouTube CPMs are described as opaque and non-transparent — do not take a single CPM as a market rate.
Results like a $2 CAC at six-figure scale come from a specific creator and were described as an outlier, not a norm.

cards.title: Is Amazon or Google Shopping Under-Weighted in Your Mix?
cards.summary: Channel mix should reflect category demand capture, not a default 'Meta-first' assumption — Google Shopping and YouTube are still major drivers for certain categories.
cards.use_when: Reviewing channel allocation for a store whose category has clear search demand (jewelry, electronics, tools) but is over-indexed on Meta.
steps: Map category demand: if buyers search for the product type (e.g., earbuds, jewelry), Google Shopping and YouTube likely deserve share.
Split paid media across Meta, Google (Shopping and YouTube), Amazon ads, and influencer so no single channel carries the whole account.
Consider that the source positions Meta at ~40–45%, Google ~20%, AppLovin 5–10%, and influencer for a portfolio spending near $100M — treat this as one operator's skew, not a target.
Re-evaluate TikTok spend explicitly: the source says they were 'sleeping on' TikTok despite evidence other operators scale on it, especially in younger-audience categories.
Reallocate based on incrementality, not legacy habit — verify with 1-day-click ROAS to compare channel-level performance over time.
caveats: The exact mix percentages are from one operator's portfolio and year.
TikTok and AppLovin channel economics change quickly — re-check current platform interfaces and reporting before making decisions.

cards.title: Attributing Operator Edge in Public 'Picks and Shovels' Stocks
cards.summary: Operators argue their inside view of platforms and DTC tools gives them an informational edge in publicly traded e-commerce derivative stocks.
cards.use_when: Considering whether personal operating experience gives a real edge when investing in public platform stocks, or evaluating whether brand association with a platform reveals underlying adoption before the market prices it in.
steps: Identify where you have direct, first-hand adoption signals — such as being a paying customer and seeing a channel cross a meaningful share of spend.
Separate two kinds of evidence: no access to internal financials, but observed strategic importance to your own business and peer operators.
Look at category-wide adoption patterns, not just a single account's data, before converting observation into a thesis.
For micro-caps, be aware that position size and volume can move the stock — the source notes this explicitly.
Default to simple, unemotional allocation strategies (S&P, golden butterfly, Ray Dalio-style portfolios) if you do not have the operator edge, rather than trading on vibes.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is not financial advice and that his investment posture is deliberately high-risk because distributions cover his burn.
Citations of specific tickers, valuations, and stock-price moves are examples from the source's experience and not endorsements or forecasts.
Public-market investment is out of scope for most operators and should not be treated as a growth lever for an ecommerce business.

cards.title: Vivid Vision: Writing a Letter to Your Future Self as an Operator
cards.summary: Writing a dated letter from your future self clarifies what business and life outcomes you are actually building toward, which then guides strategy and risk-taking.
cards.use_when: Annual or multi-year planning for an ecommerce brand — choosing which markets, channels, or business models to build toward.
steps: Pick a specific future date (e.g., a birthday 5–10 years out) and write a letter to yourself as the person you will be then.
Describe outcomes across roles: operator, owner, family member, community member — not just revenue or exit numbers.
Use the letter to define the end state you are playing toward (e.g., being recognized as a meaningful stakeholder in a category) so day-to-day decisions align with it.
Revisit the letter on a schedule and compare current strategy against it — especially when considering concentrated bets or category pivots.
Reduce friction by being specific: dates, roles, and named outcomes work better than generalized aspirations.
caveats: The source frames this as 'manifestation,' not a rigorous operating plan; treat it as a direction-setter, not a forecast.
No specific number of categories or length of letter is prescribed.

cards.title: Second-Mover Advantage in AI Adoption
cards.summary: The source argues for being a fast follower on AI tools — waiting to see what demonstrably moves profit before retooling teams around hype.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much resource to commit to AI tools and headcount for ecommerce operations, creative, and fulfillment.
steps: Define a payback test up front (source example: 'if I spend $10k on tokens I want at least $10k more in dividends').
Identify which team members already deliver real AI-driven value on operational problems, and work outward from them rather than mandating blanket rollouts.
Prioritize AI use cases tied to margin, dividend, or operating cost — not novelty adoption for its own sake.
Reassess periodically as the platform landscape shifts, since the source notes this is a fast-moving area.
caveats: The source says they had 'very little to show' from vibe-coding personally, even while eight team members were delivering — this is an honest mixed result, not a case for or against AI.
Any specific tooling or vendor mentioned may have changed — verify current interfaces before standardizing.
